answer: Twenty proposals, twenty votes, each one on chain forever. Governance vote participation history counts them: votes cast in twenty on-chain proposals. Buying a vote is cheap; buying a four-year voting history means buying tokens, holding them through crashes, and voting when nobody watches - the summit of the attack is that history has a price measured in years, not dollars. A farm needs a hundred such histories, and the timber in each is the balance that must sit still while markets move. The quill that signs the record is the chain itself: it forgets nothing and it cannot be edited.
